description: We are building "The Earth Information Jukebox" from Praia, Cape Verde! Our goal is to create a modern, intuitive, and multimedia web experience that transforms complex NASA Earth science data into engaging "tracks" that anyone can explore, visualize, and understand effortlessly. We are looking for creative minds—especially UI/UX designers, front-end developers, storytellers, and Earth science enthusiasts—who want to collaborate and turn satellite data into an accessible discovery tool!
summary:
Earth has a story. Earth Jukebox invites people to explore it through images, descriptions and sound.

Created by Praia DataJuke in Praia, Cabo Verde, this browser-based experience pairs NASA Earth science visualizations with sonification generated in real time. Eleven visualizations explore phenomena including winds, ocean currents, precipitation, aerosols and forest structure.

Visitors choose between audio-guided and visual exploration, sharing the same catalog and player. Keyboard controls, optional English narration, sound-learning examples and textual explanations support different ways of exploring. Users can select still images or available video excerpts, listen, pause, explore sampled moments, compare visual features and consult NASA sources.

The sound engine maps pixel brightness, color, highlighted-cell density and frame changes to musical parameters. It does not infer physical measurements or identify land-cover classes from colors. Sources and interpretation limits remain explicit.

Earth Jukebox aims to make Earth science more approachable for students, educators and curious explorers. Validation with blind and low-vision participants remains a next step.
details:
Earth Jukebox — By Praia DataJuke

The challenge

Earth science visualizations reveal patterns that can be difficult to understand through images alone. For people who cannot rely on vision, those patterns may be even harder to explore.

Earth Jukebox responds to The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing NASA scientific visualizations with sound generated in the browser. Our goal is to provide complementary ways to discover Earth science through imagery, text, spoken guidance and interactive sonification.

What we developed

Created in Praia, Cabo Verde, Earth Jukebox is a browser-based experience with two entry paths:

  • Explore with audio guidance: optional English narration, descriptions, sound-learning examples and guided controls.
  • Explore visually: NASA imagery, video excerpts and interactive sonification.

Both experiences share the same catalog, audio engine and playback controls. Visitors can switch experiences while preserving the selected resource, valid playback position and audio preferences.

The catalog includes eleven NASA visualizations covering winds, precipitation, nighttime lights, ocean currents, aerosols, air quality, carbon dioxide, lightning, atmospheric rivers and forest height. All include still images; ten also include short video excerpts. Resources without video are clearly identified as image only.

The homepage features an interactive decorative Earth with local imagery, rotation controls, an animation pause button and a static alternative. Its silent animated waves are decorative rather than scientific measurements.

How the sonification works

Earth Jukebox analyzes rendered visual features and converts them into musical parameters:

  • Brightness influences note pitch and intensity.
  • Color influences synthesized timbre.
  • Highlighted-cell density influences harmony and intensity.
  • Changes between sampled frames influence noise accents.

These mappings are explicit sound-design choices. The application synthesizes its own audio using Tone.js; it does not play NASA audio recordings.

Visitors can explore a still image or prepare twelve sampled moments from an available video excerpt. Playback controls, frame descriptions and visual feedback help connect what is being heard with the selected imagery.

Guided exploration

The guided experience brings selection, source choice and playback into a compact panel. Visitors can choose a visualization, select Still frame or Video frames when available, and start listening.

Additional tools include:

  • Short, clearly identified educational demonstrations of the sound mappings.
  • Playback status, pause and stop controls.
  • A “Where am I?” action that repeats the current context.
  • Descriptions of the visualization and direct access to its NASA source.
  • Previous and next sampled-frame controls.
  • Listening to a selected frame, remembering a moment and comparing it with another.

Narration can be repeated, interrupted or disabled. Text remains available when speech synthesis is unavailable. Sound does not start automatically when the homepage loads.

Scientific transparency

The engine measures pixels, not physical quantities. Brightness and color do not establish wind speed, pollutant concentration, vegetation type or other scientific measurements.

Each resource provides scientific context, source attribution, its documented period and interpretation limits. Playback time within an excerpt is distinguished from the scientific period represented.

Labels, backgrounds, camera movement and rendering choices can influence the visual features being sonified. A short excerpt is not a complete scientific time series.

NASA’s Caldwell 73 sonification is acknowledged as a conceptual reference only; its astronomical data and audio are not used.

Technology and accessibility

The application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tone.js, Three.js and Canvas 2D. Scientific media and decorative Earth textures are included locally.

Both entry paths retain images and text. Native controls, keyboard navigation, visible focus, accessible labels, loading and error messages, optional narration and reduced-motion alternatives support different interaction needs.

Automated tests cover application behavior, audio transitions, media availability, responsive layouts and browser interactions. These checks do not establish WCAG conformance. Testing with NVDA, VoiceOver and blind or low-vision participants remains necessary to validate autonomy and comprehension.

Impact and next steps

Earth Jukebox aims to help students, educators and curious explorers approach Earth science through more than one sense. Its contribution combines guided exploration, transparent visual-to-sound mappings and direct access to scientific sources.

Our next priority is human validation: observing whether people can independently choose a visualization, understand the sounds, listen, pause, explore moments and consult the source without looking at the screen.

Earth Jukebox is an independent project and is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by NASA.
